title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models

paper.title: Beyond Plausible Prediction: Safety Sufficiency in Web World Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency : whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Web agents increasingly use world models to predict the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with live websites ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Chae et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . In this setting, a world model predicts an action-conditioned future from the current context and a candidate action. Such predictions support planning, trajectory generation, agent training, and inference-time decision making ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Kazantzidis et al., 2026 ) . Yet a plausible future does not necessarily contain the information needed for the correct safety decision. Consider an agent installing a software update from an unverified third-party source. A world model may plausibly predict that “the update will be installed successfully”, while omitting that the source is unverified. The prediction may therefore plausibly describe what will happen , yet be insufficient for deciding whether it should happen . This failure can persist even when the predicted future is semantically plausible: in a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. At the same time, low unsafe-execution rates can coexist with highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour. For example, WebSynthesis-Qwen3-8B achieves a 0.08% false-safe execution rate, but 0.00% Ask recall and 99.90% Block recall (Table 1 ). Thus, avoiding unsafe execution alone does not establish whether a model correctly distinguishes permitted, clarifiable, and prohibited actions. Figure 1: Plausible futures are not necessarily safety-sufficient. A world-model prediction may plausibly describe the consequence of an action while omitting policy-decisive information needed for the downstream decision. Here, the predicted future correctly describes the software update as being installed, but omits that its source is unverified, resulting in Execute rather than the policy-consistent Block decision. We call this requirement safety sufficiency : whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required for the downstream authorisation decision. A false-safe future is one failure mode in which a plausible prediction omits such information and supports Execute when the applicable policy requires Ask or Block (Figure 1 ). Existing agent-safety benchmarks and predictive guardrails evaluate unsafe behaviour, risk, or intervention ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Tur et al., 2025 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) , but do not directly evaluate whether a world-model predictive interface supports this authorisation boundary. To address this gap, we introduce SafeWebWorld , a benchmark that jointly evaluates action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned Execute / Ask / Block decisions across five web-safety domains. The three-way decision distinguishes actions that may proceed, those requiring clarification of authority, intent, or scope, and those prohibited regardless of further confirmation. SafeWebWorld also enables us to ask whether poor authorisation behaviour can be addressed simply by improving security-evidence preservation. Under controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning (SA-SFT), evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. We call this dissociation Authorisation-Policy Collapse . This raises a further question: does authorisation-sensitive score structure disappear, or does it survive but fail to reach the emitted decision? We introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR) to distinguish these possibilities. LAR examines whether authorisation-sensitive score structure survives collapse, whether decision quality remains recoverable from frozen scores, and whether apparent recovery persists under finer-grained authorisation checks. We find that aggregate decision quality is substantially recoverable from frozen scores, with the extent of single-backbone recovery varying substantially by backbone; paired recovery provides only a modest gain beyond the strongest calibrated single-backbone readout. Yet this does not translate reliably to fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Our main contributions are: Safety sufficiency and SafeWebWorld. We formulate safety sufficiency around the information required to distinguish Execute , Ask , and Block , and introduce SafeWebWorld to evaluate it across five web-safety domains. Evidence preservation is not sufficient for authorisation. Low false-safe execution can coexist with asymmetric authorisation behaviour, while controlled SA-SFT can improve evidence preservation without reliably improving authorisation decisions. Recoverability is not sufficient for robust authorisation. LAR shows that aggregate decision quality remains recoverable from frozen scores, with the extent of single-backbone recovery varying substantially by backbone and only modest additional gain from paired recovery, while fine-grained authorisation failures persist.

sections.heading: 2.1 Web World Models and Prediction-Level Safety Evaluation
sections.text: WebArena and Mind2Web provide realistic browser-agent evaluation settings ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2023 ) . Web world models extend interaction to prediction: WMA models action-conditioned transitions for planning, while WebWorld and WebSynthesis learn web dynamics for simulation, search, and trajectory generation ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . World models also support agent self-improvement, model-based reinforcement learning, and forward-dynamics training ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026b ) ; Kazantzidis et al. (2026) combine simulation with preferences and safety justifications. Most of this work emphasises transition fidelity, planning utility, or downstream performance; False Prophets instead studies misleading predictions as an attack surface ( Imgrund et al., 2026 ) . Web-agent security benchmarks cover prompt injection, malicious websites, unsafe tool use, policy violations, and adversarial interactions ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Tur et al., 2025 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , while WebGuard evaluates predicted outcomes and risks ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Predicted consequences are used for pruning or replanning ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , risk assessment and correction ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , and joint future-state/action-risk assessment ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ; policy guardrails infer decisions from context ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Xiang et al., 2025 ) , and BadDreamer studies backdoored futures in autonomous-driving world models ( Shuai et al., 2026 ) . By contrast, SafeWebWorld directly evaluates safety sufficiency : whether an intermediate action-conditioned prediction preserves the policy-decisive evidence required to distinguish Execute , Ask , and Block before execution. A false-safe future is a plausible prediction that omits such evidence and supports Execute when Ask or Block is required.

sections.heading: 2.2 Authorisation Failure Attribution and Recovery
sections.text: Prior work on clarification, permission modelling, least privilege, abstention, and over-refusal studies when agents should ask, act, or refuse under uncertain authority or scope ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Michael and Roesner, 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2024 ) . The Authorisation–Execution Gap argues that similar failures may have different structural causes, but concerns authorisation during open-world execution rather than prediction-level attribution ( Wu et al., 2026a ) . An incorrect endpoint decision alone does not reveal whether authorisation-sensitive score structure was lost or merely mapped poorly by the decision readout. This distinction motivates separating score survival, same-backbone recoverability, paired gain, and distributional verification. Probing tests what remains decodable from frozen representations ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ; Pimentel et al., 2020 ) ; calibration remaps existing scores ( Platt and others, 1999 ; Guo et al., 2017 ) ; selective classification handles abstention and coverage ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) ; stacked generalisation combines predictive views ( Wolpert, 1992 ; Alazraki et al., 2023 ) ; and distributional analyses test gains across sources or subpopulations ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Liu and Wu, 2024 ) . Building on these controls, LAR diagnoses authorisation failures through score survival, same-backbone recovery, paired gain, and distributional diagnostics, formally defined in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 3.1 Benchmark Formulation
sections.text: SafeWebWorld evaluates prediction before execution. Given a user goal g g , security policy p p , web observation o o , and benchmark-supplied candidate action a a , the visible input is x = ( g , p , o , a ) x=(g,p,o,a) ; target, provenance, and audit fields are reserved for supervision, evaluation, and integrity checks (Appendix Table 9 ; Appendix Fig. 6 ). The reference target is y ⋆ = ( f ⋆ , e ⋆ , ℓ ⋆ , r ⋆ , d ⋆ ) y^{\star}=(f^{\star},e^{\star},\ell^{\star},r^{\star},d^{\star}) , where f ⋆ f^{\star} is a constructed action-conditioned future, e ⋆ e^{\star} the decisive security evidence derived from o o , ℓ ⋆ ∈ { safe , unsafe } \ell^{\star}\in\{\textsc{safe},\textsc{unsafe}\} the consequence class, r ⋆ ∈ { 0 , 0.8 , 1 } r^{\star}\in\{0,0.8,1\} an ordinal intervention code rather than a calibrated probability, and d ⋆ ∈ { Execute , Ask , Block } d^{\star}\in\{\textsc{Execute},\textsc{Ask},\textsc{Block}\} the policy-conditioned reference decision. The model produces a corresponding structured prediction y ^ = ( f ^ , e ^ , ℓ ^ , r ^ , d ^ ) \hat{y}=(\hat{f},\hat{e},\hat{\ell},\hat{r},\hat{d}) , where the decision field d ^ \hat{d} is evaluated rather than executed. The locked evaluator scores evidence, consequence, and decision, validates the risk field, and leaves future plausibility to the separate human evaluation. This schema separates future prediction, evidence preservation, consequence and risk output, and policy decision without ranking alternative actions or measuring end-to-end task success. Figure 2: SafeWebWorld benchmark overview: public-derived and controlled examples across five web-safety domains and three policy decisions under a unified structured-prediction schema, enabling prediction-level evaluation of safety sufficiency.

sections.heading: 3.2 Risk Taxonomy and Decision Boundary
sections.text: SafeWebWorld includes safe controls and five representative unsafe risk families: prompt injection and task hijacking , where page-level instructions attempt to override the user goal or policy; transaction and permission abuse , including unauthorised payments, subscriptions, approvals, record changes, and access grants; malicious download and redirect , involving software installation, untrusted downloads, or unsafe destinations; phishing and credential theft , where credentials or identity information are requested by an unverified or unnecessary destination; and data exfiltration and unintended disclosure , where sensitive information is transferred beyond its authorised scope. These threats overlap with prior web-agent security benchmarks ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2024 ) , while their five-family grouping and policy-conditioned annotation are specific to SafeWebWorld. Safe controls are needed because an always-block policy can achieve a low false-safe execution rate while providing little practical utility. The benchmark unit is a decision boundary , rather than a complete browser trajectory. The target decision is defined by: d ⋆ ​ ( x ) = { Execute , if ​ p ​ permits ​ a ​ without further authorisation , Ask , if ​ p ​ requires resolving authority, scope, or intent , Block , if ​ p ​ prohibits ​ a . d^{\star}(x)=\begin{cases}\textsc{Execute},&\text{if }p\text{ permits }a\text{ without further authorisation},\\ \textsc{Ask},&\text{if }p\text{ requires resolving authority, scope, or intent},\\ \textsc{Block},&\text{if }p\text{ prohibits }a.\end{cases} This three-way distinction separates unresolved authorisation from outright prohibition. Mapping Ask to Block is conservative under a binary metric but unnecessarily removes user agency; mapping Ask to Execute crosses an unresolved authorisation boundary. Consequently, an intervention is credited only when its type matches the applicable policy condition.

sections.heading: 3.3 Benchmark Construction and Validation
sections.text: SafeWebWorld combines public-derived resources with controlled scenarios, drawing on existing web-agent, world-model, and security benchmarks ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Tur et al., 2025 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2024 ; Dalton et al., 2025 ) . Public-derived examples retain source identifiers; all examples are normalised to the SafeWebWorld schema rather than treated as ready-made labels. Controlled scenarios fill uncovered risk–decision cells, increase authorisation-sensitive Ask coverage, and provide matched safe controls. Examples are assigned to source–scenario groups before splitting. With γ i \gamma_{i} denoting the group identifier of example i i , the fixed group-disjoint split enforces γ i = γ j ⇒ split ⁡ ( i ) = split ⁡ ( j ) \gamma_{i}=\gamma_{j}\Rightarrow\mathrm{split}(i)=\mathrm{split}(j) , so variants of one scenario cannot cross TRAIN, DEV, and TEST. The frozen TEST split is excluded from parameter fitting, configuration selection, and tuning. Exact- and semantic-overlap audits verify protected split pairs, and record-level audits confirm split assignments.

sections.heading: 3.4 Benchmark Statistics and Positioning
sections.text: SafeWebWorld contains 30,000 TRAIN, 1,000 DEV, and 3,000 audited TEST examples spanning five unsafe risk families and three decisions: Execute , Ask , and Block . TEST comprises 600 safe and 2,400 unsafe examples. Primary metrics are balanced accuracy and Macro-F1, with False Safe, Safe Utility, Auth-BA, Evidence Recall, and ESL as diagnostics. Appendix Table 4 reports the complete statistics and split roles. Relative to existing world-model, predictive-safety, and web-agent security evaluations, SafeWebWorld directly evaluates safety sufficiency : whether an intermediate prediction preserves policy-decisive evidence for authorisation under an explicit policy input and a structured Execute / Ask / Block decision contract. Appendix Table A.2 provides the full comparison; Appendix A documents benchmark construction, integrity, provenance, and audit results.

sections.heading: 3.5 Evaluation
sections.text: We use balanced accuracy (BA) and macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) as primary SafeWebWorld metrics and report Ask and Block recall. Malformed or incomplete outputs remain in the evaluation denominator. Authorisation Balanced Accuracy (Auth-BA) is the mean of Ask and Block recall; False-Safe Execution Rate measures gold-unsafe cases assigned Execute ; Safe Utility measures gold-safe controls retained as executable; Evidence Recall measures annotation-relative recovery of policy-decisive cues on gold-unsafe examples; and Authorisation Confusion Rates distinguish directed authorisation errors. Expected Security Loss (ESL) combines false-safe execution, unnecessary intervention, and missed evidence under the frozen cost matrix. These benchmark endpoints are distinct from the failure-attribution diagnostics introduced with LAR in Section 4 . Appendix B gives the complete metric definitions and evaluator treatment, and Table 10 summarises their units, directions, and roles.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: SafeWebWorld provides the benchmark and evaluation interface; this section presents Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR), a diagnostic framework for attributing authorisation failures in frozen models. LAR organises established score analysis, calibration, paired readouts, and distributional checks into Diagnose–Localise–Recover–Verify; DCPF instantiates the paired component of its Recover stage.

sections.heading: 4.1 Authorisation-Policy Collapse and Failure Attribution
sections.text: Let M up M_{\rm up} denote upstream structured-prediction measures, such as Evidence Recall, and let M pol M_{\rm pol} denote authorisation-decision measures, such as ASK and BLOCK recall. We define Authorisation-Policy Collapse as preserved or improved M up M_{\rm up} accompanied by degradation in an authorisation-sensitive component of M pol M_{\rm pol} . An incorrect endpoint decision does not reveal whether authorisation-sensitive score structure has been lost or whether it survives but is mapped poorly by the decision readout. After diagnosis, LAR proceeds through Localise, Recover, and Verify. First, we test whether ASK/BLOCK score separation survives in the frozen model. Second, we ask how much decision quality can be recovered by changing only the readout of the same backbone, and whether a second frozen backbone provides additional information. Third, we test whether any apparent recovery persists under distributional and matched-authorisation checks. Figure 3 summarises the analysis and Algorithm 1 specifies its DCPF instantiation. Figure 3: LAR diagnostic framework. LAR diagnoses authorisation-policy collapse (1), measures score-level separability (2) and readout recoverability (3), and verifies whether recovery survives pairing, distributional, and matched-authorisation checks (4), corresponding to Sections 4.1 – 4.4 , respectively.

sections.heading: 4.4 Does Recovery Survive Controlled Checks?
sections.text: Aggregate recovery does not by itself establish robust authorisation. A readout may exploit source, family, or scenario regularities while remaining insensitive to fine-grained changes in authority or scope. We therefore compare paired recovery against the strongest calibrated single-backbone control and evaluate whether the gain depends on correct same-example correspondence. We further test recovery under pairing nulls, group-aware holdout, source transfer, shared-wrong cohorts, mixed-label within-family evaluation, and matched authorisation conditions. We additionally use cross-fitted held-out log loss to test whether one frozen score view provides predictive information conditional on the other. Full definitions of Cross-Backbone Complementarity (CBC), Cross-fitted Conditional Predictive Gain (CCG), and the verification protocols are given in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: The frozen TEST-3000 evaluation compares Qwen3-8B/14B/32B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , Skywork-OR1-32B ( He et al., 2025 ) , WebWorld-8B/14B/32B ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) , WebSynthesis-Qwen3-8B ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and DCPF under a common visible-input and structured-output contract and a locked evaluator, with frozen model-specific prompt variants, wrappers, and decoding settings documented in Appendix C . Preserved open-model baselines are single runs; SA-SFT and DCPF report mean and sample standard deviation over seeds 42, 123, and 2027. Calibration and DCPF readouts are fitted on TRAIN, with configurations selected on DEV without best-seed selection; TEST is excluded from fitting, configuration selection, and tuning (Appendix Table 4 ). Accordingly, Figure 4 reports the DEV recovery ablation used for mechanism analysis and configuration selection, whereas Table 1 reports the frozen TEST evaluation. A protocol-matched fixed-300 evaluation additionally includes preserved GPT-5.6 ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , Claude Opus 4.8 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) , and Gemini 2.5 Pro ( Google, 2025 ) outputs. Future plausibility is evaluated on the same 300 TEST identifiers for all ten open-model baselines, yielding 3,000 matched predictions. Full inference, annotation, compute, and provenance details are provided in Appendices C , I , and L .

sections.heading: 5.5 Distributional Verification and Failure Analysis
sections.text: Aggregate recovery remains strong under group-aware separation: on the 6,580-example AUDIT_HOLDOUT , FIT-trained Llama calibration reaches 91.81 ± 2.34 % 91.81\pm 2.34\% BA, compared with 92.99 ± 2.45 % 92.99\pm 2.45\% for DCPF, leaving only a modest paired gain (Appendix Table 23 ). Source-transfer results remain strong in both directions (Appendix Table H.2 ), and on shared-wrong cases DCPF recovers at least 95.83% of Ask and retains at least 91.44% of Block cases across seeds (Appendix Table H.3 ). However, all shared-wrong Ask cases lie in transaction_permission_abuse ; within this 160-example mixed-label family, DCPF falls to 35.55% BA, 8.77% Block recall, and 0.480 ASK/BLOCK AUC, so pooled recovery does not establish fine-grained within-family authorisation identification. Figure 5 tests this boundary on 30 matched Execute / Ask / Block triplets: DCPF reaches 72.22 ± 9.62 % 72.22\pm 9.62\% ASK/BLOCK directional accuracy but only 8.89 ± 5.09 % 8.89\pm 5.09\% exact-triplet accuracy. Base Qwen and Base Llama likewise share 96.67% directional accuracy but differ sharply in exact-triplet accuracy (10.00% vs. 73.33%). Directional score movement is therefore insufficient for correct three-way authorisation decisions. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SafeWebWorld to evaluate safety sufficiency : whether plausible web-world predictions preserve the policy-decisive information needed for Execute / Ask / Block decisions. Across models, semantic plausibility, evidence preservation, and authorisation behaviour can diverge; controlled SA-SFT further shows that improving evidence preservation does not necessarily improve authorisation. LAR shows that authorisation-sensitive score structure can survive such failures and that aggregate decision quality remains recoverable from frozen scores, with strongly backbone-dependent same-backbone recovery and only modest additional gain from paired recovery. Yet fine-grained authorisation failures persist. Together, these results show that plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recoverability are distinct properties, and none is sufficient on its own for robust authorisation. Limitations and scope. SafeWebWorld is an offline diagnostic benchmark rather than an estimate of failure prevalence in live deployment, and its five risk families are not intended as a universal web-safety taxonomy. The human study evaluates semantic plausibility rather than observed rollout accuracy, while LAR is studied primarily with two frozen 8B backbones. The matched-authorisation evaluation is a controlled diagnostic rather than an estimate of real-world failure rates.

sections.heading: A.1 Motivation and Interface
sections.text: SafeWebWorld asks whether a plausible predicted future is safety-sufficient: whether it retains the evidence needed for a policy-conditioned decision. Each example exposes only ( g , p , o , a ) (g,p,o,a) —task goal, policy, observation, and candidate action—and requires a future, security evidence, consequence, risk, and decision; construction fields, targets, provenance, and risk-family labels remain hidden. EXECUTE applies when policy permits the action, ASK when intent, authority, authorisation, or scope is unresolved but clarifiable, and BLOCK when an invariant restriction prohibits it. This three-way distinction prevents binary safe/unsafe evaluation from conflating clarification with refusal. sections.heading: A.3 Construction and Provenance
sections.text: Table 4 consolidates the frozen benchmark overview, split sizes, fitting roles, audited TEST composition, risk coverage, decision labels, and evaluation measures. The corpus combines public-derived web tasks with controlled cases designed to cover consequential policy boundaries. Records retain provenance and construction metadata for auditing, but these fields are excluded from inference. Source groups are assigned before splitting to reduce direct scenario leakage. sections.heading: B.2 LAR Operational Metrics
sections.text: LPS, LRG, CBC, and CCG are proposed authorisation-specific operational metrics for failure attribution rather than benchmark endpoints. LPS measures ASK/BLOCK separability in the frozen semantic-score margin; LRG measures recovery from changing the readout of the same frozen backbone; CBC isolates paired gain beyond the strongest calibrated single-backbone control; and CCG measures the cross-fitted held-out log-loss reduction obtained by adding one frozen score view conditional on the other. LPS is reported as ROC-AUC, LRG and CBC as percentage-point differences when applied to percentage metrics, and CCG as log-loss reduction. These quantities use established statistical primitives but are ordered by LAR to distinguish score survival, same-backbone recoverability, and incremental paired information. sections.heading: D.3 LPS properties
sections.text: LPS AB is the probability that a randomly selected gold-ASK example receives a higher ASK-minus-BLOCK margin than a randomly selected gold-BLOCK example, with conventional tie handling. It is invariant to strictly monotone transformations of the scalar margin. This ranking property does not identify where a signal is represented internally and does not guarantee useful separation within every family.

sections.text: LRG M and CBC M inherit the units and behaviour of M M . A gain in balanced accuracy need not imply a gain in BLOCK recall or expected loss. Accordingly, all paired claims name the metric and retain class-wise ASK/BLOCK reporting. No confidence interval is assigned to CBC; the frozen comparisons report point differences across the predeclared three-seed means.

Under unrestricted population log loss, a Bayes-risk identity motivates a connection to conditional mutual information. sections.text: Each expert receives the same visible tuple. Semantic decision scores sum the full token sequence for EXECUTE, ASK, and BLOCK conditioned on the expert’s frozen generated prefix. Within-expert log-normalisation prevents direct comparison of uncalibrated vocabulary-logit scales across tokenisers.

sections.heading: E.2 Readout and objective
sections.text: For TRAIN example i i , let h i = h ⁡ ( x i ) ∈ ℝ 6 h_{i}=h(x_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{6} denote the concatenated frozen score vector and let y i ∈ { E , A , B } y_{i}\in\{E,A,B\} denote its reference decision class. The concatenated six-dimensional vector feeds an affine 6 → 3 6\to 3 map with bias: 18 weights and three biases. For TRAIN class count n c n_{c} , total N N , and three classes, the class-balanced weight is w c = N / ( 3 ​ n c ) w_{c}=N/(3n_{c}) and the fitted objective is ℒ DCPF = − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N w y i log softmax ( W h i + b ) y i . \mathcal{L}_{\rm DCPF}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{y_{i}}\log\operatorname{softmax}(Wh_{i}+b)_{y_{i}}. (21) The TRAIN counts E = 6000 E=6000 , A = 4080 A=4080 , and B = 19920 B=19920 give weights 1.666667, 2.450980, and 0.502008. Only the 18 weights and three biases are trainable. The Qwen and Llama parameters remain frozen and are not merged.

sections.heading: E.3 Seeds and Reload Validation
sections.text: Separate heads are fitted for seeds 42, 123, and 2027 using matched SA-SFT experts. Reload validation confirms that persisted heads reproduce the frozen readout.

sections.heading: E.4 Upstream invariance
sections.text: For every DEV and TEST row in all three seeds, DCPF future, security evidence, consequence, and risk equal the paired Qwen SA-SFT fields. The mismatch count is zero for each field. DCPF therefore changes policy calibration without modifying upstream world/evidence generation. Because the evidence field is unchanged, Evidence Recall is exactly inherited from Qwen SA-SFT. False Safe, Safe Utility, and ESL are numerically unchanged on the frozen TEST evaluation; we report that empirical equality rather than attributing it solely to upstream-field invariance.

sections.heading: E.5 Cost
sections.text: DCPF adds only 21 fitted parameters but requires semantic scoring from two frozen 8B backbones. Parameter efficiency should not be confused with inference efficiency: runtime and memory cost exceed those of either single-backbone control.

sections.text: Paired performance can arise from the marginal score distributions of two models or from same-example correspondence. A pairing null separates these possibilities without retraining either backbone.

sections.heading: Objective.
sections.text: The structured evaluation measures whether a model preserves policy-decisive evidence and produces the benchmark-required authorisation decision. It does not directly measure whether the predicted future is semantically plausible. We therefore evaluate whether model-generated futures describe plausible direct consequences of candidate actions, including in cases whose gold decision requires Ask or Block .

sections.heading: Models and sampling.
sections.text: We evaluate the ten open-model baselines reported in Table 1 . The same 300 TEST identifiers are used for every model, producing 3,000 model–ID prediction pairs. This matched design holds the underlying TEST cases fixed across models. The study uses preserved model outputs; no model was retrained or rerun for this evaluation.

sections.heading: Annotation unit.
sections.text: Each annotation unit contains the benchmark context, candidate action, model-generated predicted_future , and constructed reference_future . The annotator determines whether the predicted future describes a plausible direct consequence of executing the candidate action in the given context. The reference future provides a task-specific expected consequence but is not treated as an observed post-action state or rollout outcome.

sections.heading: Annotation rubric.
sections.text: Each prediction is assigned one of three labels: Pass , Fail , or Uncertain . • Pass : the prediction describes a semantically plausible, action-conditioned consequence. It need not match the reference wording, but it must preserve the principal action, affected object or party, and resulting state change. • Fail : the prediction contradicts the action or context, omits its essential consequence, introduces an unsupported outcome, follows an unrelated instruction, or merely restates the current state. • Uncertain : the available information is insufficient or the prediction is too ambiguous for a reliable Pass / Fail judgement. Plausibility is assessed independently of writing style, lexical overlap, and safety. A Pass label means that the predicted consequence is plausible, not that the action is authorised or secure.

sections.heading: Human review and quality control.
sections.text: The primary annotator reviewed all 3,000 prediction pairs with AI assistance. AI assistance was used to organise the displayed evidence, apply the fixed rubric consistently, and flag potentially ambiguous or inconsistent cases; all reported labels were reviewed and confirmed by the human annotator. A second human annotator reviewed a blinded, overlapping subset of 150 predictions, also with AI assistance. This subset was used to assess annotation consistency and did not add new TEST cases. Differences and uncertain cases were resolved through human review under the same rubric. Eight initially uncertain primary annotations were adjudicated as Fail ; the remaining Pass / Fail labels were unchanged.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Across the 3,000 model–ID pairs, 2,583 predictions (86.10%) are labelled plausible and 417 are labelled implausible. Among the plausible predictions, 2,076 of 2,583 (80.37%) correspond to gold-unsafe cases requiring Ask or Block . Equivalently, plausible predictions in gold-unsafe cases account for 69.20% of all evaluated pairs. Model-level matched results are reported in Table 26 . Plausibility ranges from 73.00% to 97.00% across the ten models. On the 240 gold-unsafe identifiers within the same matched cohort, Evidence Recall ranges from 22.81% to 38.12%, while False Safe ranges from 0.00% to 8.33%. These results show that high semantic plausibility can coexist with limited annotation-relative recovery of policy-decisive evidence and, for some systems, false-safe execution. sections.heading: Relationship to structured safety metrics.
sections.text: The human validation complements the full structured TEST-3000 evaluation. For the matched analysis in Table 26 , Evidence Recall and False Safe retain their benchmark definitions and are recomputed on the 240 gold-unsafe Ask / Block cases within the same 300-identifier cohort. False Safe measures the proportion of gold-unsafe examples assigned Execute , whereas Evidence Recall measures annotation-relative recovery of benchmark-required security evidence. The human study instead measures whether a predicted consequence is semantically plausible. These metrics therefore capture distinct properties: semantic plausibility, evidence preservation, and downstream unsafe execution. The plausibility and gold-unsafe proportions must not be interpreted as additional false-safe rates.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The study assesses textual predictions rather than outcomes observed after executing actions in a live environment. The constructed reference future is not an independently observed post-action state. The study also does not annotate policy-evidence omission at the individual prediction level; Evidence Recall is obtained from the separate structured evaluation. The results therefore support claims about semantic plausibility and its prevalence in benchmark gold-unsafe cases, but not claims about real-world rollout accuracy, evidence sufficiency, or authorisation correctness.

sections.heading: L.1 Seed and Freeze Protocol
sections.text: All trained-method summaries report seeds 42, 123, and 2027 with sample standard deviation; no best seed is selected. SA-SFT checkpoints and DCPF heads are frozen before the reported TEST inference. Calibration and DCPF parameters are fitted on TRAIN, configuration selection uses DEV, and TEST is used for neither fitting, selection, nor tuning. DCPF reload validation and upstream-invariance checks are completed before aggregation.

sections.heading: L.2 Fixed-300 Subset Procedure
sections.text: The ordered cohort contains 300 unique TEST identifiers. For each seed, stable-identifier matching selects exactly 300 existing DCPF TEST-3000 predictions, with no missing or duplicate matches. Selection does not modify prediction content. The fixed-300 evaluator is then applied to the selected subset. No additional backbone inference, DCPF inference, refitting, or subset-specific model selection is performed.

sections.heading: L.3 TEST Disclosure
sections.text: The Qwen SA-SFT TEST results were observed before the LAR/DCPF extension was conceived. TEST-3000 therefore serves as a frozen historical and descriptive evaluation rather than an untouched DCPF method-conception holdout. The primary mechanism claims rely on DEV and the group-aware evaluations rather than on treating TEST as an unseen method-development set.

sections.heading: L.4 Compute and Software Environment
sections.text: Most open-model training and inference experiments were run on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80GB memory on an anonymised institutional high-performance computing cluster. A single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti SUPER GPU with 16GB VRAM was used for limited local development, validation, and smaller-scale runs. The software environment used PyTorch 2.5.1, CUDA 12.4, and PyTorch Geometric 2.6.1. Experiment configurations and software environments were frozen in the corresponding manifests. No institution, cluster name, user path, or allocation identifier is required for reproducing the reported experimental protocol. Closed-source rows are derived from preserved historical API outputs rather than rerun during the present evaluation.

Cristea Affiliation: Durham University Adel Bibi Affiliation: University of Oxford Jialin Yu Affiliation: University of Oxford Abstract Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency : whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation. A Preprint 1 Introduction Web agents increasingly use world models to predict the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with live websites ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Chae et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . In this setting, a world model predicts an action-conditioned future from the current context and a candidate action. Such predictions support planning, trajectory generation, agent training, and inference-time decision making ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026b ; Kazantzidis et al., 2026 ) . Yet a plausible future does not necessarily contain the information needed for the correct safety decision. Consider an agent installing a software update from an unverified third-party source. A world model may plausibly predict that “the update will be installed successfully”, while omitting that the source is unverified. The prediction may therefore plausibly describe what will happen , yet be insufficient for deciding whether it should happen . This failure can persist even when the predicted future is semantically plausible: in a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. At the same time, low unsafe-execution rates can coexist with highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour. For example, WebSynthesis-Qwen3-8B achieves a 0.08% false-safe execution rate, but 0.00% Ask recall and 99.90% Block recall (Table 1 ). Thus, avoiding unsafe execution alone does not establish whether a model correctly distinguishes permitted, clarifiable, and prohibited actions. Figure 1: Plausible futures are not necessarily safety-sufficient. A world-model prediction may plausibly describe the consequence of an action while omitting policy-decisive information needed for the downstream decision. Here, the predicted future correctly describes the software update as being installed, but omits that its source is unverified, resulting in Execute rather than the policy-consistent Block decision. We call this requirement safety sufficiency : whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required for the downstream authorisation decision. A false-safe future is one failure mode in which a plausible prediction omits such information and supports Execute when the applicable policy requires Ask or Block (Figure 1 ). Existing agent-safety benchmarks and predictive guardrails evaluate unsafe behaviour, risk, or intervention ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Tur et al., 2025 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) , but do not directly evaluate whether a world-model predictive interface supports this authorisation boundary. To address this gap, we introduce SafeWebWorld , a benchmark that jointly evaluates action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned Execute / Ask / Block decisions across five web-safety domains. The three-way decision distinguishes actions that may proceed, those requiring clarification of authority, intent, or scope, and those prohibited regardless of further confirmation. SafeWebWorld also enables us to ask whether poor authorisation behaviour can be addressed simply by improving security-evidence preservation. Under controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning (SA-SFT), evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. We call this dissociation Authorisation-Policy Collapse . This raises a further question: does authorisation-sensitive score structure disappear, or does it survive but fail to reach the emitted decision? We introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR) to distinguish these possibilities. LAR examines whether authorisation-sensitive score structure survives collapse, whether decision quality remains recoverable from frozen scores, and whether apparent recovery persists under finer-grained authorisation checks. We find that aggregate decision quality is substantially recoverable from frozen scores, with the extent of single-backbone recovery varying substantially by backbone; paired recovery provides only a modest gain beyond the strongest calibrated single-backbone readout. Yet this does not translate reliably to fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Our main contributions are: Safety sufficiency and SafeWebWorld. We formulate safety sufficiency around the information required to distinguish Execute , Ask , and Block , and introduce SafeWebWorld to evaluate it across five web-safety domains. Evidence preservation is not sufficient for authorisation. Low false-safe execution can coexist with asymmetric authorisation behaviour, while controlled SA-SFT can improve evidence preservation without reliably improving authorisation decisions. Recoverability is not sufficient for robust authorisation. LAR shows that aggregate decision quality remains recoverable from frozen scores, with the extent of single-backbone recovery varying substantially by backbone and only modest additional gain from paired recovery, while fine-grained authorisation failures persist. 2 Related Work 2.1 Web World Models and Prediction-Level Safety Evaluation WebArena and Mind2Web provide realistic browser-agent evaluation settings ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2023 ) . Web world models extend interaction to prediction: WMA models action-conditioned transitions for planning, while WebWorld and WebSynthesis learn web dynamics for simulation, search, and trajectory generation ( Chae et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . World models also support agent self-improvement, model-based reinforcement learning, and forward-dynamics training ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026b ) ; Kazantzidis et al. (2026) combine simulation with preferences and safety justifications. Most of this work emphasises transition fidelity, planning utility, or downstream performance; False Prophets instead studies misleading predictions as an attack surface ( Imgrund et al., 2026 ) . Web-agent security benchmarks cover prompt injection, malicious websites, unsafe tool use, policy violations, and adversarial interactions ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Tur et al., 2025 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , while WebGuard evaluates predicted outcomes and risks ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Predicted consequences are used for pruning or replanning ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , risk assessment and correction ( Shen et al., 2026 ) , and joint future-state/action-risk assessment ( Yu et al., 2026 ) ; policy guardrails infer decisions from context ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Xiang et al., 2025 ) , and BadDreamer studies backdoored futures in autonomous-driving world models ( Shuai et al., 2026 ) . By contrast, SafeWebWorld directly evaluates safety sufficiency : whether an intermediate action-conditioned prediction preserves the policy-decisive evidence required to distinguish Execute , Ask , and Block before execution. A false-safe future is a plausible prediction that omits such evidence and supports Execute when Ask or Block is required. 2.2 Authorisation Failure Attribution and Recovery Prior work on clarification, permission modelling, least privilege, abstention, and over-refusal studies when agents should ask, act, or refuse under uncertain authority or scope ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Michael and Roesner, 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2024 ) . The Authorisation–Execution Gap argues that similar failures may have different structural causes, but concerns authorisation during open-world execution rather than prediction-level attribution ( Wu et al., 2026a ) . An incorrect endpoint decision alone does not reveal whether authorisation-sensitive score structure was lost or merely mapped poorly by the decision readout. This distinction motivates separating score survival, same-backbone recoverability, paired gain, and distributional verification. Probing tests what remains decodable from frozen representations ( Hewitt and Liang, 2019 ; Pimentel et al., 2020 ) ; calibration remaps existing scores ( Platt and others, 1999 ; Guo et al., 2017 ) ; selective classification handles abstention and coverage ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) ; stacked generalisation combines predictive views ( Wolpert, 1992 ; Alazraki et al., 2023 ) ; and distributional analyses test gains across sources or subpopulations ( Chen et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Liu and Wu, 2024 ) . Building on these controls, LAR diagnoses authorisation failures through score survival, same-backbone recovery, paired gain, and distributional diagnostics, formally defined in Section 4 . 3 SafeWebWorld 3.1 Benchmark Formulation SafeWebWorld evaluates prediction before execution. Given a user goal g g , security policy p p , web observation o o , and benchmark-supplied candidate action a a , the visible input is x = ( g , p , o , a ) x=(g,p,o,a) ; target, provenance, and audit fields are reserved for supervision, evaluation, and integrity checks (Appendix Table 9 ; Appendix Fig. 6 ). The reference target is y ⋆ = ( f ⋆ , e ⋆ , ℓ ⋆ , r ⋆ , d ⋆ ) y^{\star}=(f^{\star},e^{\star},\ell^{\star},r^{\star},d^{\star}) , where f ⋆ f^{\star} is a constructed action-conditioned future, e ⋆ e^{\star} the decisive security evidence derived from o o , ℓ ⋆ ∈ { safe , unsafe } \ell^{\star}\in\{\textsc{safe},\textsc{unsafe}\} the consequence class, r ⋆ ∈ { 0 , 0.8 , 1 } r^{\star}\in\{0,0.8,1\} an ordinal intervention code rather than a calibrated probability, and d ⋆ ∈ { Execute , Ask , Block } d^{\star}\in\{\textsc{Execute},\textsc{Ask},\textsc{Block}\} the policy-conditioned reference decision. The model produces a corresponding structured prediction y ^ = ( f ^ , e ^ , ℓ ^ , r ^ , d ^ ) \hat{y}=(\hat{f},\hat{e},\hat{\ell},\hat{r},\hat{d}) , where the decision field d ^ \hat{d} is evaluated rather than executed. The locked evaluator scores evidence, consequence, and decision, validates the risk field, and leaves future plausibility to the separate human evaluation. This schema separates future prediction, evidence preservation, consequence and risk output, and policy decision without ranking alternative actions or measuring end-to-end task success. Figure 2: SafeWebWorld benchmark overview: public-derived and controlled examples across five web-safety domains and three policy decisions under a unified structured-prediction schema, enabling prediction-level evaluation of safety sufficiency. 3.2 Risk Taxonomy and Decision Boundary SafeWebWorld includes safe controls and five representative unsafe risk families: prompt injection and task hijacking , where page-level instructions attempt to override the user goal or policy; transaction and permission abuse , including unauthorised payments, subscriptions, approvals, record changes, and access grants; malicious download and redirect , involving software installation, untrusted downloads, or unsafe destinations; phishing and credential theft , where credentials or identity information are requested by an unverified or unnecessary destination; and data exfiltration and unintended disclosure , where sensitive information is transferred beyond its authorised scope. These threats overlap with prior web-agent security benchmarks ( Levy et al., 2026 ; Evtimov et al., 2025 ; Debenedetti et al., 2024 ; Zhan et al., 2024 ) , while their five-family grouping and policy-conditioned annotation are specific to SafeWebWorld. Safe controls are needed because an always-block policy can achieve a low false-safe execution rate while providing little practical utility. The benchmark unit is a decision boundary , rather than a complete browser trajectory. The target decision is defined by: d ⋆ ​ ( x ) = { Execute , if ​ p ​ permits ​ a ​ without further authorisation , Ask , if ​ p ​ requires resolving authority, scope, or intent , Block , if ​ p ​ prohibits ​ a . d^{\star}(x)=\begin{cases}\textsc{Execute},&\text{if }p\text{ permits }a\text{ without further authorisation},\\ \textsc{Ask},&\text{if }p\text{ requires resolving authority, scope, or intent},\\ \textsc{Block},&\text{if }p\text{ prohibits }a.\end{cases} This three-way distinction separates unresolved authorisation from outright prohibition. Mapping Ask to Block is conservative under a binary metric but unnecessarily removes user agency; mapping Ask to Execute crosses an unresolved authorisation boundary. TEST comprises 600 safe and 2,400 unsafe examples. Primary metrics are balanced accuracy and Macro-F1, with False Safe, Safe Utility, Auth-BA, Evidence Recall, and ESL as diagnostics. Appendix Table 4 reports the complete statistics and split roles. Relative to existing world-model, predictive-safety, and web-agent security evaluations, SafeWebWorld directly evaluates safety sufficiency : whether an intermediate prediction preserves policy-decisive evidence for authorisation under an explicit policy input and a structured Execute / Ask / Block decision contract. Appendix Table A.2 provides the full comparison; Appendix A documents benchmark construction, integrity, provenance, and audit results. 3.5 Evaluation We use balanced accuracy (BA) and macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) as primary SafeWebWorld metrics and report Ask and Block recall. Malformed or incomplete outputs remain in the evaluation denominator. Authorisation Balanced Accuracy (Auth-BA) is the mean of Ask and Block recall; False-Safe Execution Rate measures gold-unsafe cases assigned Execute ; Safe Utility measures gold-safe controls retained as executable; Evidence Recall measures annotation-relative recovery of policy-decisive cues on gold-unsafe examples; and Authorisation Confusion Rates distinguish directed authorisation errors. Expected Security Loss (ESL) combines false-safe execution, unnecessary intervention, and missed evidence under the frozen cost matrix. These benchmark endpoints are distinct from the failure-attribution diagnostics introduced with LAR in Section 4 . LAR organises established score analysis, calibration, paired readouts, and distributional checks into Diagnose–Localise–Recover–Verify; DCPF instantiates the paired component of its Recover stage. 4.1 Authorisation-Policy Collapse and Failure Attribution Let M up M_{\rm up} denote upstream structured-prediction measures, such as Evidence Recall, and let M pol M_{\rm pol} denote authorisation-decision measures, such as ASK and BLOCK recall. We define Authorisation-Policy Collapse as preserved or improved M up M_{\rm up} accompanied by degradation in an authorisation-sensitive component of M pol M_{\rm pol} . An incorrect endpoint decision does not reveal whether authorisation-sensitive score structure has been lost or whether it survives but is mapped poorly by the decision readout. After diagnosis, LAR proceeds through Localise, Recover, and Verify. First, we test whether ASK/BLOCK score separation survives in the frozen model. Second, we ask how much decision quality can be recovered by changing only the readout of the same backbone, and whether a second frozen backbone provides additional information. Third, we test whether any apparent recovery persists under distributional and matched-authorisation checks. Figure 3 summarises the analysis and Algorithm 1 specifies its DCPF instantiation. Aggregate recovery does not by itself establish robust authorisation. A readout may exploit source, family, or scenario regularities while remaining insensitive to fine-grained changes in authority or scope. We therefore compare paired recovery against the strongest calibrated single-backbone control and evaluate whether the gain depends on correct same-example correspondence. Across models, semantic plausibility, evidence preservation, and authorisation behaviour can diverge; controlled SA-SFT further shows that improving evidence preservation does not necessarily improve authorisation. LAR shows that authorisation-sensitive score structure can survive such failures and that aggregate decision quality remains recoverable from frozen scores, with strongly backbone-dependent same-backbone recovery and only modest additional gain from paired recovery. Yet fine-grained authorisation failures persist. Together, these results show that plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recoverability are distinct properties, and none is sufficient on its own for robust authorisation. Limitations and scope. SafeWebWorld is an offline diagnostic benchmark rather than an estimate of failure prevalence in live deployment, and its five risk families are not intended as a universal web-safety taxonomy. The human study evaluates semantic plausibility rather than observed rollout accuracy, while LAR is studied primarily with two frozen 8B backbones. The matched-authorisation evaluation is a controlled diagnostic rather than an estimate of real-world failure rates. All research design, core annotations, candidate validation, reported measurements, and scientific interpretations were independently conducted or reviewed by the authors. Appendix A SafeWebWorld Benchmark Specification and Integrity A.1 Motivation and Interface SafeWebWorld asks whether a plausible predicted future is safety-sufficient: whether it retains the evidence needed for a policy-conditioned decision. Each example exposes only ( g , p , o , a ) (g,p,o,a) —task goal, policy, observation, and candidate action—and requires a future, security evidence, consequence, risk, and decision; construction fields, targets, provenance, and risk-family labels remain hidden. EXECUTE applies when policy permits the action, ASK when intent, authority, authorisation, or scope is unresolved but clarifiable, and BLOCK when an invariant restriction prohibits it. This three-way distinction prevents binary safe/unsafe evaluation from conflating clarification with refusal.
